https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/2.heading: Fighting rages near Yemen’s Taiz as UN urges humanitarian access | Conflict News | Al Jazeera
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/2.body:
Fighting has escalated in Yemen, with media affiliated to government forces reporting a surge in hostilities with the Houthis on several fronts south of Taiz in southwestern Yemen.

Yemen Today TV reported on Thursday that fighting was taking place on the Al-Aqroudh and Al-Masrakh fronts, as well as in Al-Rahn village in the Sabir al-Mawadim district.

Houthi-affiliated media reported four air strikes against the city of Mocha and its port on the Red Sea, west of Taiz.

Yemeni government forces in Taiz said they repelled attacks on Al-Aqroud, as they tried to break the Houthi siege of the area.

“Our forces have carried out 749 military operations over the past 24 hours, resulting in the death or injury of 239 militants and the destruction of 117 vehicles and armoured vehicles,” Majid al-Nazili, a spokesman for Yemeni government forces, told Al Jazeera.

The Houthis – also known as Ansar Allah, Arabic for Supporters of God – also advanced on Jabal Sabr on Sunday, the strategic mountain overlooking Taiz. It has become the focus of the fighting between the Iran-backed group and forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised government, backed by Saudi Arabia.

Meanwhile, flights have resumed at Aden international airport, the Anadolu news agency reported. Services were suspended on Wednesday after witnesses said a missile had landed on the Al-Nasr Camp, adjacent to the airport, where Yemeni coastguard forces and interior ministry headquarters are located.

A military source told Al Jazeera on Thursday that government forces carried out three air strikes against Houthi military gatherings and vehicles southeast of Taiz, claiming that they targeted the group’s positions and movements on the Al-Aqroud front. This comes as the Houthi group reported more than 100 air strikes targeting the capital city Sanaa, and eight other Yemeni governorates, over the past 24 hours.

The surge in fighting across multiple fronts in Yemen has worsened a spiralling humanitarian crisis.

The conflict has forced more than 281,000 people from their homes in Yemen since the beginning of August, according to the United Nations’ humanitarian agency.

The Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned that “time is running out” to deliver aid to the 800,000 people trapped inside the city of Taiz.

Humanitarian access has become increasingly difficult over the past three weeks, OCHA said, due to damage to a key road linking Taiz to southern governorates. Aid supplies now have to pass narrow mountain routes to reach people in need.

OCHA called on fighters not to target civilians or aid convoys. “All parties must respect international humanitarian law and allow safe, sustained and unimpeded humanitarian access so that aid can reach people in need,” it said.

The war in Yemen has escalated sharply since the Houthis seized strategic territory from government forces along the Red Sea coast last month, prompting a counteroffensive. Saudi Arabia has since intensified its strikes on the group.

Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, which is aligned with Yemen’s government forces, have dealt a blow to the kingdom, the world’s biggest exporter of crude oil, disrupting its businesses, airlines and residents, and damaging its international image.

https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/un-co.heading: UN condemns U.S. economic embargo of Cuba though more nations sit out amid Trump push | PBS News
https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/un-co.body:
UNITED NATIONS (AP) — The U.N. General Assembly condemned the U.S. economic embargo of Cuba for the 34th year on Wednesday, even as Washington's campaign to influence the outcome led to a number of countries voting against the resolution or sitting out the decision for the first time.

WATCH: Trump at GOP rally in Florida revives idea of military intervention in Cuba after Iran

The vote was 130-17, with 25 abstentions — a notable decrease in support from last year, when more than 160 nations supported the measure and only 12 abstained. While such resolutions at the U.N. General Assembly are not legally binding, they do reflect world opinion.

For the first time in 34 years, Western countries like Germany, Italy and Latvia were among those that refrained from voting. Bosnia, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Lithuania, Morocco, North Macedonia, Paraguay and Slovenia are among those member states that voted no — most for the first time.

It marks a stunning shift in international support at a time when the small island country weathers outages, shortages and other deepening financial troubles as the Trump administration looks to force changes to Cuba's political system by increasing an already punishing economic campaign. President Donald Trump last week once again raised the specter of U.S. military intervention, saying American warships could stop over in Cuba on their way back from the Iran war.

"A great power is attacking through economic war a member state of this organization," Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez said ahead of the vote. "Cuba is not a threat. The blockade is a threat."

U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz told member nations that, "your vote today is the only thing standing between the corrupt, kleptocratic communist regime and using this body and your vote for another propaganda victory at the expense of the Cuban people."

Tensions between Washington and Havana have spilled over into fiery public spats at the United Nations. On Tuesday, Waltz and Rodríguez got into a shouting match on the floor of the General Assembly while debating the embargo resolution.

Shortly after Waltz had begun his criticism of the socialist government, Rodríguez walked down to the podium where the U.S. envoy was addressing the hall and called him a liar while trying to get a point of order from the official presiding over the session.

"This individual needs to back away from this podium. He's not going to intimidate me in the United States of America," Waltz said as U.N. security and personnel tried to intervene. "You understand who you're dealing with? This is America. Back up."

In a post on X, Rodríguez reminded Waltz where he was making his remarks, saying he's at the U.N., not at a national security meeting at the White House.

"With his crude lies at the UN General Assembly, the U.S. government has launched another desperate attempt to justify its economic aggression against Cuba and its criminal energy blockade," he continued.

On the sidelines of the GA hall, Waltz accused a member of Cuba's delegation of attacking an American diplomat who was filming him. He said Secretary of State Marco Rubio has ordered the official sent home. The State Department on Wednesday confirmed to the AP that the individual accused has left the U.S.

A week earlier, a similar interaction between Waltz and his Cuban counterpart, Ernesto Soberón Guzmán, took place outside a U.S.-hosted panel with Cuban dissidents and former prisoners that sought to highlight allegations of the oppressive behavior of the island's government.

It all reflects a clear break from the traditional diplomatic decorum expected at the U.N. and the new phase of contentiousness between the U.S. and Cuba.

The U.S. embargo against Cuba was first imposed in 1960 after Fidel Castro led a revolution that toppled dictator Fulgencio Batista and nationalized properties belonging to U.S. citizens and corporations.

As a result, the Caribbean country has spent decades facing the dire impact of longtime economic and financial troubles and is now being pushed to a breaking point after Trump announced in late January that he would impose tariffs on any country that sells or provides oil to Cuba.

The warning has effectively cut off fuel to the island, leading to widespread power outages that impact basic services such as water supply and internet and telephone services.

Associated Press writer Matthew Lee in Washington and Dánica Coto in San Juan, Puerto Rico, contributed to this report.

Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue.

https://www.defensenews.com/global/europ.heading: NATO’s Black Sea nations decry Ukraine war spillover endangering commercial ship traffic - Defense News
https://www.defensenews.com/global/europ.body:
IZMIR, Turkey — The Ministers of Defense of Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey have condemned attacks against commercial vessels in the Black Sea and call on all parties to refrain from any further actions that could endanger commercial vessels, maritime infrastructure and freedom of navigation in the Black Sea, according to the joint statement made after a meeting in Sofia, Bulgaria, on Oct. 28.

The trilateral meeting on security in the Black Sea region was also attended by the Chiefs of Defense of Bulgaria and Turkey, Adm. Emil Eftimov and Gen. Selcuk Bayraktaroglu, and the Deputy Chief of Defense of Romania, Lt. Gen. Dragos Dimitru Iakub.

The meeting signals a coordinated approach by the three NATO littoral states to the growing risks to commercial shipping and maritime infrastructure arising from the Russia-Ukraine war.

The Financial Times reported based on data from maritime security company Ambrey and the International Maritime Organization (IMO) that since the beginning of the year, more than 570 vessels have been hit in the Black Sea, killing at least 40 seafarers. By comparison, 24 deaths have been recorded in the Strait of Hormuz area for the same period.

The joint declaration highlights the Black Sea’s importance for global trade and the supply of grain fertilizers and recalls that all parties must comply with international law, including the Montreux Convention and applicable international humanitarian law, to ensure security in the Black Sea and preserve regional stability.

Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey also agreed to enhance information and intelligence sharing, improving maritime domain awareness and strengthening early warning to support security and stability in the Black Sea.

Turkish Defense Minister Yaşar Güler stated after the meeting that Turkey will maintain its current implementation of the Montreux Convention.

“I believe that the united and resolute position we have demonstrated here today, in full coordination and solidarity with our friends and allies Bulgaria and Romania, is important in clearly reminding both warring parties that the security of commercial shipping routes in the Black Sea and the safety of littoral countries constitute inviolable red lines,” Güler said.

The Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov stated that the three Black Sea countries will continue active cooperation both in a trilateral format and within NATO, in close coordination with the member states and partners of the alliance.

As the ministerial meeting was convening in Sofia, the Bulgarian Navy reported that it has successfully conducted a rescue operation for the crew of the Liberian flag merchant ship Contship Jet after it was hit by an unmanned surface vessel. The ship was 17 miles east of Cape Kaliakra in Bulgaria and bound for the port of Constanta in Romania.

The three countries will continue consultations, with the next round scheduled to take place in Ankara and Bucharest.

https://www.rfi.fr/en/middle-east/202610.heading: IMF says engaging with Iraq on preparing new bailout program
https://www.rfi.fr/en/middle-east/202610.body:
Washington (United States) (AFP) – The International Monetary Fund on Thursday said it was engaging with Iraqi authorities as it prepares a new bailout program for the country, whose economy has been battered by the war on Iran.

The US-Israel war on Iran, launched in late February, plunged the region into conflict and saw Tehran's retaliatory action virtually block the Strait of Hormuz, a key energy supply route.

Iraq's economy is heavily dependent on its energy exports, which almost entirely rely on transport through the strait.

Before the war, the country was already facing acute fiscal constraints, and the IMF this month forecast its economy would contract by 16 percent this year.

"Our plan now is to engage with the authorities to understand better their priorities, how they want to address their vulnerabilities, and then to move ahead on how we can best support them with a program," said IMF spokesperson Julie Kozack at a regular press briefing in Washington.

Kozack cited the country's severe financing constraints from before the outbreak of the war, and said its very narrow non-oil revenue base was also putting pressure on the fiscal balance.

The last of Iraq's three most recent programs with the IMF ended in 2019.

It has a total of around $428 million in interest payments due to the Fund by 2030, according to IMF data.

IMF Chief Kristalina Georgieva first disclosed that Iraq had approached the Fund for a new program at the Fund's annual meetings in Bangkok earlier this month.

At those meetings, Georgieva lauded the resilience of global economic growth in the face of wars in Iran and Ukraine, but warned that outcomes were highly uneven with more vulnerable economies battered hard by the conflicts.
